processing: Made as a green tea, despite the name: "white" refers to the pale spring shoots of an albino plant. It comes in two shapes, pine-needle and flat.
harvest_season: Spring only, with a picking and production window of less than a month. The 2025 season opened in late March. The shoots lose their pale colour as temperatures rise.
appearance_dry: Neat, whole leaf in mixed yellow and green, shaped either as fine needles or flat blades.
appearance_liquor: Bright and clear, in a pale green-yellow.
appearance_wet: Tender, even and glossy shoots in light yellow-green.
taste_profile: Fresh and brothy, high-scented and smooth, with a sweet return and only a faint astringency.

brewing.notes: Treat it as a delicate green tea. Glass shows off the leaf, and cooler water keeps the savoury sweetness from going flat.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, since the albino window is so short. Grades are special, first and second, in needle or flat shape. Drink it within the year, as with other delicate greens.
description:
This is the trap in the name: Zheng'an White Tea is a green tea. It comes from Zheng'an county in northern Guizhou, and it is called white because the plant's spring shoots grow pale, not because it is made like Fuding or Zhenghe white tea.

The paleness is a seasonal albino effect. In cool early spring the shoots fail to make chlorophyll normally, and once it warms the leaf turns green again. That leaves a picking season of under a month, and the leaf made in that window is rich in amino acids, which is where the brothy sweetness comes from.

The cup is bright and fragrant, savoury-sweet and smooth, with very little bitterness. Brew it like a fine green tea, in cooler water, and do not leave the leaf sitting in the pot.

It is sold in needle-shaped and flat forms, in three grades, under a protected place name and various company brands. Buy this year's spring tea and check it says Zheng'an, because many other teas with the white-tea name are unrelated.
history:
Zheng'an White Tea received national geographic indication protection on 12 May 2011, covering 19 towns and townships of the county, at gardens around 800 to 1100 metres. Tea growing in the county is described locally as more than a thousand years old.

A local legend links the tea to Yin Zhen, the Eastern Han scholar from this area, who is said to have carried home-grown tea when he visited the great teacher Xu Shen. It is a story of regional pride and says nothing reliable about this modern cultivar-based tea. In recent years the county has built up the public brand, with over a hundred company labels beneath it.
